items.title: Rufus Reid interviewed by Monk Rowe, Atlanta, GA, January 4, 2013
items.q: And then you turn around and you read the typical “jazz is dead” article or — Gary Giddins said something about how can you promote this music when it’s not on radio or TV etcetera.

ctx.x: you’ve been supporting all that. And then there’s nobody to support you when you play. And that can be a drag sometimes. And so we try to — well either I’m saying, well I don’t want to solo. Because sometimes the bass solo tanks that energy that has been already established. So I don’t want to do that too. If I’m going to do it, I want to help make it go too. So it’s a decision sometimes, and my ego — I like to solo, I want to solo, and I think I play better solos than I used to. But most people don’t hire me to…

Let’s talk about this conference we’re at. It’s an interesting state of affairs in jazz it seems like. If you come here — I just came from this little gathering of people talking about research. And in that room there was at least four or five different accents of people. In other words it was like an international group of people. And you’ve got I don’t know how many people here, and it makes jazz look really vibrant and healthy. And then you turn around and you read the typical “jazz is dead” article or — Gary…

Well he just doesn’t know. I don’t know why or even how or why he would even make such a statement because he obviously hasn’t been or doesn’t see the things that I see, and see what a lot of other — it’s a different time than when the music that even like what you presented with Joe Williams — that’s a different era. It was a different place. And even before that, that music was really popular. I mean the pop music of that day. We’ve lost that. I mean even Broadway, because a lot of those songs came through…
